newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.S.and EU trumpet breakthrough on trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S.and EU trumpet breakthrough on trade.

text.p: The United States and the European Union said Wednesday they had cleared the way for a deal under which approval of safety standards by one country would be accepted by others in five product categories.

"We feel that we have a breakthrough and we hope that it will lead to an agreement in the next few days," President Clinton said after EU-U.S. talks with Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok and European Commission President Jacques Santer.
The two sides also signed a cooperation accord on controlling chemicals used to make synthetic drugs and a customs deal Kok said would boost trade and help fight fraud and graft.
He said the two sides had also bridged bilateral differences on animal inspections, preventing a possible trans-Atlantic wrangle on meat quality standards.
"We also reached an agreement on veterinary inspection, thus resolving a trade conflict that might otherwise have arisen on the export of meat products," Kok said.
While the customs cooperation and drug precursor deals were flagged well in advance of Wednesday's summit, the one on so-called Mutual Recognition Agreements came as more of a surprise.
Both Kok and Santer echoed Clinton's assessment of such a deal being but a few days away, but European Commission officials warned that any text still had to go to EU capitals.
Mutual Recognition Agreements are expected to cut manufacturers' marketing costs by up to 10 percent by allowing each party to recognise the other's testing, inspection and certification procedures.
A U.S. official said ahead of the talks that Mutual Recognition Agreements on product standards had been sorted within the final hours.
The official said MRAs would reduce marketing costs for telecommunications equipment, information-technology products, pharmaceuticals, medical devices and pleasure boats.
Final sticking points concerned U.S. Food and Drug Administration regulation of pharmaceuticals and medical devices.

He said the FDA was legally prohibited from ceding final inspection authority over the manufacturing of these devices, but as a practical matter would not have to strictly follow the law in the case of already-approved products manufactured under EU standards.
